The volume theorem tracks the finite-dimensional coordinate-change constant, while the density pushforward lemmas integrate each parameter fiber. The preceding factorization leaves a density proportional to \(M(\theta)^N\), with the scaling and coordinate-change factors independent of \(\theta\). Normalization cancels those positive finite factors exactly, yielding \[(p_\theta)_\#\Pi_N(d\theta)=\frac{M(\theta)^N\,d\theta}{\int M(u)^Ndu}.\] The final target probability and moment lemmas are consequences of this identity and the already proved lifted target facts.

Formal correspondence: marginalTarget : The parameter law with density proportional to the N th power of the original latent marginal. This names the statistical target without assuming anything about its concentration.

Let \(J=N^{-Nd_x/2}\) denote the total latent dilation factor. Up to the fixed coordinate-volume constant, the projected unnormalized density is \(J M(\theta)^N\). Its integral over parameter space has the same prefactor. Dividing these two expressions proves the normalized density formula. In particular the parameter mode is a maximizer of \(M\), because raising a positive number to the positive integer \(N\) preserves order.

steps.title: Normalize the power target and guard its moments
steps.body:
The established projection identity and the probability property of \(\Pi_N\) prove that \(\pi_N^\theta\) is a probability measure. Its unnormalized density \(M^N\) is everywhere positive, so its extended partition is strictly positive. If that partition were infinite, the definition of the normalized target would be the zero measure, contradicting mass one; thus it is also finite. Finally the lifted Gibbs law has a finite second moment and \(p_\theta\) is a bounded linear map. The pushforward integral identity therefore gives \(\theta\mapsto\theta\in L^2(\pi_N^\theta)\). This supplies finite marginal moments before the later sharp bound is applied.

Formal correspondence: marginalTarget_isProbability : The marginal power density normalizes to a probability measure as a consequence of its proved equality with the actual Gibbs projection. marginalPartition_pos : The normalizer of the powered marginal density is strictly positive. marginalPartition_ne_top : The powered marginal partition is finite. Its proof uses the previously established probability identity, so divergence cannot disappear in a real conversion or an infinite normalizing constant. marginalTarget_memLp : The parameter marginal has finite second moment, without a separate marginal moment or concentration assumption.

The lifted Gibbs law already has mass one, so its measurable projection does too. A hypothetical infinite marginal partition would make its normalized density zero and hence give total mass zero, a contradiction. Finally, \(\|p_\theta z\|^2\le\|z\|^2\) transfers the lifted second moment through the projection. This gives the finite marginal moments needed before a quantitative concentration radius is introduced.

IPLA/PrekopaLeindler.lean.title: One-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler by constructed monotone transport
IPLA/PrekopaLeindler.lean.summary:
For positive continuous densities in one dimension, cumulative distribution functions provide an explicit monotone change of variables. The proof uses the derivative of this change of variables and the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. It then removes normalization to obtain an inequality between arbitrary positive finite integrals, ready for the marginal-convexity argument.

The proof constructs transport directly from cumulative integrals of positive continuous densities. It derives the one-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler inequality without postulating a transport map or marginal log-concavity theorem.

steps.title: Cumulative integrals are differentiable and strictly increasing
steps.body:
A density here is a continuous strictly positive real function \(f\), integrable on \(\mathbb R\), with \(\int f=1\). Define \(F(x)=\int_{(-\infty,x]}f\). The difference formula

\[F(y)-F(0)=\int_0^y f(t)dt\]

and the fundamental theorem of calculus give the strict derivative \(F'(x)=f(x)\). Differentiability implies continuity, and positivity of the derivative implies strict monotonicity. The density assumptions are precisely the inputs required for these assertions.

Formal correspondence: Density : A positive, continuous probability density on the real line. cumulative : Cumulative integral of an ordinary real density.

For \(y>x\), the increment \(F(y)-F(x)=\int_x^y f(t)dt\) is positive because the density is positive and continuous on a nonempty interval. Thus strict monotonicity also has a direct integral interpretation. The derivative identity follows locally from the fundamental theorem of calculus; the improper lower limit contributes only a constant and does not affect differentiation.

steps.title: The cumulative range is exactly the open unit interval
steps.body:
Integrability implies \(F(x)\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\). Splitting the total integral at \(x\) gives \(F(x)=1-\int_{(x,\infty)}f\), so \(F(x)\to1\) as \(x\to+\infty\). Nonnegativity gives \(0\le F\le1\); strict monotonicity, comparing \(x\) with \(x-1\) and \(x+1\), improves this to \(0

The endpoint limits identify the inverse's correct domain: neither zero nor one is attained at a finite point. For any interior probability level, choose sufficiently far left and right points using those limits, then use continuity to obtain a preimage. Strict monotonicity makes this preimage unique. Consequently the inverse cumulative map used in transport is well defined everywhere it is needed.

steps.title: Construct and differentiate the monotone transport
steps.body:
For two densities with cumulative maps \(F,G\), set \(T=G^{-1}\circ F\), using the inverse function on its range. Since both ranges are \((0,1)\), \(G(T(x))=F(x)\) everywhere. Strict monotonicity makes \(G\) injective. The one-dimensional inverse function theorem applies because \(G'(T(x))=g(T(x))>0\), and the chain rule yields

\[T'(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(T(x))}>0.\]

Thus \(T\) is strictly increasing, and the density ratio is a proved derivative of an explicitly constructed function.

For positive continuous unit-mass densities, \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf\) and \(G(y)=\int_{-\infty}^yg\) are differentiable with strictly positive derivatives, hence strictly increasing, and their limits give range \((0,1)\). Define \(T=G^{-1}\circ F\), so \(G(T(x))=F(x)\). The inverse-function derivative gives \(T'(x)=f(x)/g(T(x))>0\). The cumulative identities and strict monotonicity declarations justify this change of variables on the whole real line.

Formal correspondence: transport : The monotone transport from density f to density g .

The identity \(G(T(x))=F(x)\) matches the mass lying to the left of corresponding points. Differentiating gives \(g(T(x))T'(x)=f(x)\); positivity of the denominator allows division and shows that the transport preserves orientation. This also proves the density Jacobian relation needed in the integral calculation, without assuming a transport existence theorem as an extra analytic premise.

steps.title: The normalized inequality is a change-of-variables calculation
steps.body:
Assume \(0\le t\le1\) and \(h((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}g(y)^t\). Put \(S(x)=(1-t)x+tT(x)\) and \(r=f(x)/g(T(x))>0\). Then \(S'=1-t+tr>0\), and convexity of the exponential gives \(r^t\le1-t+tr=S'\). At \(y=T(x)\), the pointwise premise therefore implies

\[f(x)=f(x)^{1-t}g(T(x))^t r^t\le h(S(x))S'(x).\]

Since \(S\) is strictly increasing, the one-dimensional Jacobian theorem changes the right-hand integral to the integral of \(h\) over \(S(\mathbb R)\). Nonnegativity then bounds it by the integral over all \(\mathbb R\), proving \(1\le\int h\). The formal conclusion uses an extended nonnegative integral, so \(h\) need not itself be integrable or continuous.

Set \(S(x)=(1-t)x+tT(x)\). The interpolation hypothesis bounds \(h(S(x))\) below by \(f(x)^{1-t}g(T(x))^t\). Weighted arithmetic–geometric mean gives \(S'(x)=(1-t)+tT'(x)\ge T'(x)^t\). Since \(T'=f/g(T)\), multiplication yields \(h(S(x))S'(x)\ge f(x)\). The strictly increasing change-of-variables formula then proves \(\int h\ge\int f=1\). For arbitrary positive finite masses, divide \(f,g\) by their integrals, apply the normalized statement, and multiply back; logarithmic mass terms recover \((\int f)^{1-t}(\int g)^t\).

Formal correspondence: normalized_prekopa_leindler : The normalized one-dimensional Prékopa--Leindler inequality, proved by the constructed monotone transport. The third weight need not be continuous or integrable; the conclusion is an extended nonnegative integral.

The scalar inequality \((1-t)+tr\ge r^t\) holds for every \(r>0\), including \(t=0,1\). Substitution of \(r=f/g(T)\) converts the interpolation lower bound into an exact density comparison after multiplication by the Jacobian. Integrating over the image of the increasing map is enough: nonnegativity of \(h\) bounds that image integral by the integral on the entire line. Surjectivity of the interpolating map is therefore unnecessary.

steps.title: Remove the unit-integral normalization
steps.body:
An everywhere positive integrable function on a nonzero measure space has strictly positive integral, since its support has positive measure. For the Prékopa weights write \(A=\int f>0\), \(B=\int g>0\), and \(C=A^{1-t}B^t>0\). Apply the normalized inequality to \(f/A\), \(g/B\), and \(h/C\). Expanding \(\log(f/A)=\log f-\log A\) verifies its pointwise premise. If \(h\) is nonnegative and integrable, the extended conclusion converts to \(1\le(\int h)/C\). Multiplication by \(C\) gives

\[\exp\!\left((1-t)\log\int f+t\log\int g\right)\le\int h.\]

The positivity lemma also applies to the zero-dimensional product measure needed later.

Formal correspondence: integral_positive : Strict positivity of the real integral of an everywhere positive integrable function, including the zero-dimensional product space used in tensorization. prekopa_leindler_real : Prékopa--Leindler on the real line for arbitrary positive continuous integrable first and second weights. No normalization is assumed.

Scaling \(f\) and \(g\) to unit integral changes the interpolation factor by \(A^{1-t}B^t\). The normalized result gives a lower bound of one for the integral of the correspondingly scaled third function. Multiplying by this strictly positive finite factor restores the original masses. Writing powers as exponentials of logarithms makes the endpoint weights unambiguous and uses only logarithms of positive numbers.

IPLA/PrekopaTensorization.lean.title: Finite-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler with Gaussian tails
IPLA/PrekopaTensorization.lean.summary:
The dimension induction requires a class of functions stable under marginalization. Continuous positive functions with Gaussian upper tails have exactly the needed properties: every coordinate slice is integrable, its integral varies continuously, and the resulting marginal again has Gaussian tails. This closes the induction without assuming marginal continuity or integrability independently.

Positive continuous weights dominated by an integrable Gaussian form a class closed under integrating out one coordinate. This supplies all continuity and integrability facts needed to iterate the one-dimensional transport proof.

steps.title: Gaussian domination proves integrability and positive integral
steps.body:
Write \(\mathrm{Coordinates}(n)=\mathbb R^n\). A Gaussian weight satisfies continuity, strict positivity, and \(f(x)\le Ce^{-a\sum_i x_i^2}\), with \(C,a>0\). The Euclidean Gaussian integral is finite, and the coordinate identification preserves volume, so domination proves \(f\in L^1\). Positivity on the whole nonzero volume space proves \(\int f>0\). Multiplying by \(c>0\) preserves these properties and changes the envelope constant to \(cC\).

Formal correspondence: GaussianWeight : The class of positive continuous weights with a Gaussian upper bound.

A Gaussian envelope with coefficient \(a>0\) has finite integral on \(\mathbb R^n\), as follows by the product of one-dimensional Gaussian integrals. Since the function is nonnegative, domination proves its absolute integrability. Strict positivity then makes its integral positive. Multiplication by a positive scalar preserves all three properties and changes only the envelope constant, a fact needed when strong convexity supplies an exponential prefactor.

steps.title: A coordinate slice and its marginal are integrable and continuous
steps.body:
The insertion map \((s,x)\mapsto(s,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is continuous coordinate by coordinate. Define \(f_1(x)=\int_\mathbb R f(s,x)ds\). Since \(\sum_i(s,x)_i^2=s^2+\sum_i x_i^2\ge s^2\), every slice is bounded by \(Ce^{-as^2}\), which is integrable independently of \(x\). Slice continuity supplies measurability and domination proves slice integrability. If \(x_j\to x\), joint continuity gives pointwise convergence in \(s\), and the same Gaussian bound allows dominated convergence. Hence \(f_1\) is continuous.

Write a point in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) as \(\operatorname{cons}(z,x)\), where \(z\in\mathbb R\) is the coordinate being integrated. The coordinate-insertion continuity theorem checks its first and remaining coordinates separately. A Gaussian weight has constants \(C,a>0\) satisfying

\[0<f(\operatorname{cons}(z,x))\le C\exp\!\left[-a\left(z^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2\right)\right]\le C e^{-az^2}.\]

The last inequality drops a nonnegative sum of squares, so the majorant is independent of \(x\). It is integrable in \(z\) by the one-dimensional Gaussian integral theorem. The declaration slice_integrable uses positivity to identify the absolute value of the slice with the slice itself, continuity to obtain measurability, and this majorant to prove integrability.

Now let \(x_m\to x\). For every fixed \(z\), continuity of \(f\) and of coordinate insertion gives \(f(\operatorname{cons}(z,x_m))\to f(\operatorname{cons}(z,x))\). The same Gaussian majorant controls every term and the limit. Dominated convergence therefore gives convergence of their real integrals, proving continuity of the first marginal. In the Lean invocation of continuous_of_dominated, the four obligations are slice measurability, the uniform almost-everywhere bound, integrability of that bound, and pointwise continuity in the remaining coordinates. Those are all established before the induction later treats the marginal as another Gaussian weight.

Formal correspondence: continuous_cons : Continuity of inserting the first real coordinate. firstMarginal : Integrate out the first coordinate of a weight.

The crucial majorant is independent of the remaining coordinates. Therefore a sequence of such coordinates changes only the integrand, not the integrable bound used in dominated convergence. Each slice is positive and continuous in the integrated coordinate, so its integral is positive and finite. The argument proves joint analytic control needed to regard the first marginal as a function in the same class.

steps.title: Coordinate integration preserves Gaussian tails and total integral
steps.body:
Retaining the full Gaussian envelope and factoring its exponent gives

\[f_1(x)\le C\left(\int_\mathbb R e^{-as^2}ds\right)e^{-a\sum_i x_i^2}.\]

The new constant is positive and finite, and integrating the positive slice makes \(f_1\) positive everywhere. Together with continuity, this proves that \(f_1\) is again a Gaussian weight. The coordinate splitting equivalence preserves product volume. Its integral formula and Fubini, justified by the Gaussian integrability already proved, then show \(\int f_1=\int f\).

Retaining the remaining-coordinate Gaussian factor gives a sharper conclusion than slice integrability alone. The new envelope constant is the old constant multiplied by \(\int e^{-as^2}ds\), while the decay coefficient \(a\) is unchanged. Fubini then identifies the marginal's total integral with the original integral because Gaussian domination has already established absolute integrability. These facts make repeated coordinate integration legitimate.

steps.title: Induct on the dimension
steps.body:
For \(n=0\), the coordinate space is a singleton with volume one; each integral equals its function value and the result is the pointwise premise. For dimension \(n+1\), fix remaining-coordinate vectors \(x,y\). The one-dimensional theorem applied to the slices \(s\mapsto f(s,x)\), \(r\mapsto g(r,y)\), and \(u\mapsto h(u,(1-t)x+ty)\) gives the pointwise Prékopa inequality for \(f_1,g_1,h_1\). These marginals are Gaussian weights, so the induction hypothesis applies in dimension \(n\). Replace their integrals by those of the original weights to obtain

\[\left(\int f\right)^{1-t}\left(\int g\right)^t\le\int h.\]

The formal statement writes positive powers using exponentials and logarithms, including \(t=0\) and \(t=1\).

The induction splits \(\mathbb R^{d+1}\) into its first coordinate and \(d\) remaining coordinates. For fixed remaining coordinates, apply the proved one-dimensional inequality to the first-coordinate slices. Their integrals define marginal functions that satisfy the same interpolation inequality in \(d\) dimensions. Gaussian domination proves slice integrability, continuity of those marginal functions by dominated convergence, and Gaussian tails for them. The induction hypothesis applies, and Fubini identifies the iterated integrals with the original total integrals. Dimension zero is the one-point base case.

Formal correspondence: prekopa_leindler : The finite-dimensional Prékopa--Leindler inequality. The induction uses the proved real-line transport theorem and integrates one coordinate at a time.

At the induction step the original pointwise hypothesis holds for every pair of first coordinates and every pair of remaining-coordinate vectors. Fixing the latter pair gives exactly the one-dimensional interpolation premise. Its conclusion is the corresponding premise for the marginal functions. Applying the induction hypothesis integrates the remaining coordinates, and the total-integral identities replace each iterated integral by its original multidimensional value.

IPLA/StrongLogConcavity.lean.title: Derived strong convexity of the actual marginal potential
IPLA/StrongLogConcavity.lean.summary:
Joint strong convexity is preserved when latent variables are integrated out, provided the parameter quadratic deficit is retained in the interpolation argument. The positive finite marginal integrals permit the Prékopa inequality to be converted into the strong-convexity inequality for \(-\log M\). This establishes both the correct concentration potential and uniqueness of the statistical maximizer.

Let \(M(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\) and \(\Phi(\theta)=-\log M(\theta)\). The proved finite-dimensional Prékopa–Leindler theorem shows that \(\Phi\) retains the original joint strong-convexity constant \(m\).

steps.title: Define a legitimate logarithmic marginal potential
steps.body:
The real marginal integral \(M\) is defined from the original slice; the earlier domination theorem makes it finite and strictly positive. Thus \(\Phi=-\log M\) is an ordinary real-valued continuous function: continuity follows by composing the continuous marginal with logarithm away from zero. If \(\theta_*\) maximizes the extended marginal, its finite real representation and monotonicity of logarithm imply \(\Phi(\theta_*)\le\Phi(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\). No logarithm of zero or infinite partition is used.

Formal correspondence: marginalIntegral : The real latent partition. Positivity and finiteness were proved from the joint assumptions in MarginalConcentration.lean . marginalPotential : The actual marginal negative log-likelihood, with the observations fixed. marginalMaximizer_minimizes_potential : The statistical marginal maximizer minimizes the actual negative log-likelihood. All real conversions use proved positive finite partitions.

The marginal potential is defined on all parameter values because \(0

steps.title: Prepare Gaussian weights in product coordinates
steps.body:
Define \(f_\theta(x)=e^{-U(\theta,x)}\) in ordinary finite-product coordinates, using the volume-preserving Euclidean identification for the latent block. The joint Gaussian domination gives \(f_\theta(x)\le Ce^{-m\|x\|^2/4}\), and continuity plus strict positivity make it a Gaussian weight. Its integral equals \(M(\theta)\) by the volume-preserving change of coordinates. Finally pairing preserves subtraction and affine combinations coordinatewise:

\[\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)-\operatorname{pair}(\theta',y)=\operatorname{pair}(\theta-\theta',x-y),\]\[\operatorname{pair}(a\theta+b\theta',ax+by)=a\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x)+b\operatorname{pair}(\theta',y).\]

Formal correspondence: latentWeight : A latent slice written in ordinary product coordinates for applying the finite-dimensional Prékopa--Leindler theorem.

The latent coordinate identification is volume preserving, so it changes neither the marginal integral nor its dimension. The affine pairing identity allows joint strong convexity to be applied at \((\theta,x)\) and \((\theta',y)\). Its squared difference separates into the parameter and latent squares. This separation is what permits the latent penalty to be dropped while retaining the exact parameter modulus.

steps.title: Apply Prékopa with the parameter convexity penalty
steps.body:
Let \(a,b\ge0\), \(a+b=1\), \(\theta_r=a\theta+b\theta'\), and \(c=(mab/2)\|\theta-\theta'\|^2\). Strong convexity of \(U\), the affine pair identity and norm splitting imply

\[aU(\theta,x)+bU(\theta',y)\ge U(\theta_r,ax+by)+c,\]

after discarding the nonnegative latent penalty \((mab/2)\|x-y\|^2\). Exponentiate and apply Prékopa–Leindler with third weight \(e^{-c}f_{\theta_r}\), which remains a Gaussian weight. This gives \(M(\theta)^aM(\theta')^b\le e^{-c}M(\theta_r)\). All factors are positive, so take logarithms and negate to conclude

\[\Phi(a\theta+b\theta')\le a\Phi(\theta)+b\Phi(\theta')-\frac{mab}{2}\|\theta-\theta'\|^2.\]

Thus marginal strong convexity is a theorem of the joint assumptions.

For \(\theta_r=a\theta+b\vartheta\), \(a+b=1\), joint strong convexity yields \[U(\theta_r,ax+by)\le aU(\theta,x)+bU(\vartheta,y)-\tfrac{mab}{2}\|\theta-\vartheta\|^2,\] after dropping the additional nonnegative latent deficit. Thus the latent weights satisfy the Prékopa hypothesis with the multiplier \(e^{-c}\), \(c=mab\|\theta-\vartheta\|^2/2\), on the interpolated weight. Integrating gives \(M(\theta)^aM(\vartheta)^b\le e^{-c}M(\theta_r)\).

Every marginal integral is already finite and positive, so logarithms preserve the inequality. Negating gives \(F(\theta_r)\le aF(\theta)+bF(\vartheta)-c\), exactly \(m\)-strong convexity of \(F=-\log M\). The code's hpoint is the weight inequality, hpl its Prékopa integral consequence, and hlog its logarithmic conversion. Strict convexity for \(m>0\) then proves uniqueness of the previously constructed maximizer.

Formal correspondence: marginalPotential_strongConvex : Integrating out the latent variables preserves precisely the original strong-convexity constant. This is the derived Prékopa theorem for IPLA.

Let \(c=(mab/2)\|\theta-\theta'\|^2\). The joint inequality implies \(e^{-c}e^{-U(\theta_r,ax+by)}\ge e^{-aU(\theta,x)}e^{-bU(\theta',y)}\). Prékopa therefore gives \(e^{-c}M(\theta_r)\ge M(\theta)^aM(\theta')^b\). Taking logarithms yields \(\log M(\theta_r)\ge a\log M(\theta)+b\log M(\theta')+c\). Negating this is precisely strong convexity with modulus \(m\), including the quadratic factor \(1/2\).

steps.title: The marginal maximizer exists uniquely
steps.body:
Because \(m>0\), the proved \(m\)-strong convexity makes \(\Phi\) strictly convex. Two marginal maximizers are both global minimizers of \(\Phi\); if distinct, the midpoint strict-convexity inequality would lie strictly below their common minimum, a contradiction. Hence they coincide. The earlier continuity-and-tail argument already supplied existence of a maximizer. Combining existence with this uniqueness yields \(\exists!\theta_*\) satisfying the original statistical maximizer predicate.

Formal correspondence: marginalMaximizer_unique : Joint strong convexity implies uniqueness of the marginal maximizer. existsUnique_marginalMaximizer : The marginal maximizer exists uniquely under exactly the original joint potential assumptions.

If two distinct minimizers existed, their midpoint would have value at most their common minimum minus \((m/8)\|\theta-\theta'\|^2\), strictly smaller because \(m>0\). This contradiction proves uniqueness. Existence came earlier from continuity and Gaussian decay, so the two arguments serve different purposes: coercive tails provide attainment, while the marginal interpolation inequality prevents multiple maximizing parameters.

IPLA/Concentration.lean.title: The dimension-sharp equilibrium parameter concentration
IPLA/Concentration.lean.summary:
The parameter target is a Gibbs law in parameter dimension alone, with potential \(N\Phi\). Its strong-convexity constant grows linearly with particle count. Applying the available continuous-potential concentration theorem and then transferring through the exact parameter projection produces the equilibrium term in the strongly convex particle error bound.

The exact parameter marginal has density proportional to \(M(\theta)^N=e^{-N\Phi(\theta)}\). Its potential is \(Nm\)-strongly convex in dimension \(d_\theta\), giving the equilibrium radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) without a separate concentration hypothesis.

steps.title: Identify the scaled marginal potential and its Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Multiply the strong-convexity inequality for \(\Phi\) by the nonnegative scalar \(N\). Every affine term and the quadratic penalty scale by \(N\), so \(N\Phi\) is \(Nm\)-strongly convex. Since \(M>0\),

\[e^{-N\Phi(\theta)}=e^{N\log M(\theta)}=M(\theta)^N.\]

The finite-real representation of the original extended marginal identifies this weight exactly with the one defining marginalTarget. Its normalized law is therefore the shared Gibbs measure of \(N\Phi\).

Formal correspondence: scaled_marginalPotential_strongConvex : Multiplying the actual marginal potential by N multiplies its proved strong-convexity constant by N . marginalTarget_eq_gibbsMeasure : The normalized powered marginal density is exactly the Gibbs law of the proved N -scaled negative log marginal.

The identity \(e^{-N\Phi}=M^N\) holds pointwise because \(M\) is finite and positive. Hence the two unnormalized measures, not merely their modes, coincide. Their normalizations coincide as well. This justifies applying a Gibbs concentration theorem directly to the statistical marginal target and explains why its potential has modulus \(Nm\).

steps.title: A dilation estimate gives the sharp parameter moment
steps.body:
A marginal maximizer \(\theta_*\) minimizes \(\Phi\), hence also \(N\Phi\). The shared continuous strongly convex Gibbs theorem, which needs continuity and a mode rather than differentiability of \(\Phi\), bounds the squared distance by twice dimension over convexity:

\[\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\pi_N^\theta(\theta)\le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}.\]

Apply it to the continuous potential \(N\Phi\), use the proved \(Nm\)-strong convexity, and rewrite its Gibbs law by the preceding identity. Only the parameter dimension enters; latent dimension does not enlarge this equilibrium radius.

Formal correspondence: marginalTarget_secondMoment_le : Exact finite second-moment bound about any parameter maximizing the actual latent marginal. Its existence and uniqueness were proved separately.

The estimate here is the established bound with factor two. It uses only continuity, positive strong convexity and an actual minimizing point of the marginal potential. It therefore remains applicable without proving that the marginal potential is differentiable. The latent variables have already been integrated away, so the dimension in the numerator is \(d_\theta\); replacing it by the enlarged state dimension would unnecessarily weaken the statistical concentration estimate.

steps.title: Transfer the marginal moment to the lifted Gibbs target
steps.body:
The exact projection identity \(p_{\theta\#}\Pi_N=\pi_N^\theta\) and the measurable pushforward integral formula yield

\[\int\|p_\theta z-\theta_*\|^2d\Pi_N(z)\le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}.\]

The projected Gibbs variable is already in \(L^2\), and subtracting the constant \(\theta_*\) preserves this. The shared projected-RMS theorem converts the real moment inequality to the extended RMS bound

\[\operatorname{RMS}_{\Pi_N}(p_\theta-\theta_*)\le\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}.\]

The radius is nonnegative and its square equals the moment bound, so the square-root step is legitimate. This term needs joint differentiability and strong convexity, with no gradient-Lipschitz premise.

Powering the marginal density by \(N\) multiplies its negative log potential by \(N\), so its modulus becomes \(Nm\). The actual marginal maximizer minimizes that potential. The dilation concentration theorem used in this module bounds its parameter second moment by \(2d_\theta/(Nm)\), and the exact parameter pushforward identity gives the same moment under the lifted Gibbs law. The final square-root estimate uses the proved finite second moment to interpret projected \(L^2\) error as an ordinary integral. The stronger \(d_\theta/(Nm)\) constant is separately proved in the proximal sharp-concentration extension.

Formal correspondence: gibbsTarget_parameter_secondMoment_le : Transfer the proved marginal moment bound to the actual scaled IPLA Gibbs measure using the exact parameter-marginal identity. gibbsTarget_parameter_concentration : The equilibrium concentration input in IPLA Theorem 1 is a proved theorem of the original joint assumptions. No gradient-Lipschitz or marginal assumption is needed for this statistical term.

For the nonnegative observable \(g(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2\), the pushforward identity gives \(\int g(p_\theta z)d\Pi_N=\int g(\theta)d\pi_N^\theta\). Thus the same finite upper bound is valid in the enlarged space without estimating latent deviations. Taking its nonnegative square root yields the equilibrium RMS radius. This radius can then be added to a full-state coupling error by Minkowski's inequality.

IPLA/Theorem.lean.title: The standalone strongly convex IPLA error bound
IPLA/Theorem.lean.summary:
The final inequality separates three causes of parameter error: finite-particle equilibrium spread, incomplete relaxation from the initial law, and Euler discretization. Each is controlled by a different proved ingredient. The enlarged geometry and the exact algorithm-law identification allow these ingredients to be combined in the physical parameter and particle dimensions stated in the theorem.

For the fixed observed-data slice \(U_y\), assume differentiability, joint \(m\)-strong convexity with \(m>0\), \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(N>0\), and \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L)\). Initialization is square integrable, and innovations have the stated independent standard Gaussian coordinate laws and initialization independence. Let \(\theta_*\) maximize the actual latent marginal. The theorem applies to every pair of independent natural dimensions, including zero.

steps.title: Combine lifted transport with proved equilibrium concentration
steps.body:
Suppose the state has at least one coordinate. The lifted geometry gives \(Nm\)-strong convexity and \(NL\)-smoothness in dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). The Gibbs theorem normalizes \(\Pi_N\), while square-integrable initialization and Gibbs moments imply finite initial transport. Apply the shared Gaussian ULA theorem at step \(h=\gamma/N\), using the supplied Gaussian hypotheses. The step restriction rescales exactly and gives

\[W_2(\rho_k,\Pi_N)\le(1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\mu_0,\Pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The ULA output-finiteness result and the proved law identity ensure this is finite actual transport, before any real conversion. The equilibrium concentration theorem gives \(\operatorname{RMS}_{\Pi_N}(p_\theta-\theta_*)\le\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\). For any coupling of \(\rho_k\) and \(\Pi_N\), Minkowski and \(\|p_\theta\|\le1\) imply the sampled parameter RMS is at most coupling RMS plus that equilibrium radius. Taking the coupling infimum and using finiteness yields

\[\left(\int\|p_\theta z-\theta_*\|^2d\rho_k\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\mu_0,\Pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma.\]

Stationarity, finite transport and concentration are derived here through the shared and particle theorems; they are not additional theorem hypotheses.

The proof first constructs target probability and initial finite transport from the lifted strong-convexity assumptions and \(L^2\) initialization. Gaussian ULA then gives the state-space transport rate, with step \(\gamma/N\), modulus \(Nm\), score constant \(NL\), and dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\). The law adapter identifies its output with the actual supplied IPLA recursion and proves the output transport distance is finite.

The projection inequality gives \(R_{\theta_*}(\rho_k)\le W_2(\rho_k,\Pi_N)+R_{\theta_*}(\Pi_N)\); equilibrium concentration supplies the second term. The facts houtput and hmoment ensure finite values before projected RMS is rewritten as a square-root integral. Finally, the exact particle/time scaling simplifies the transport terms. Thus normalization, stationary reference and parameter concentration are derived inputs, while joint strong convexity, smoothness and the Gaussian innovation laws remain the stated assumptions.

Formal correspondence: nonempty_dimension_bound : For fixed observations y , write U y (pair theta x) = -log p_theta(x,y) . The general-dimension counterpart of equation (34), with independent parameter dimension dtheta and latent dimension dx , for the actual Gaussian IPLA recursion and its defined Gibbs target. Every hypothesis is displayed here or is one of the Gaussian-law and independence fields of GaussianInnovations , whose definition is included in the standalone file. Normalization, all finite transport moments, a stationary Langevin reference, and the equilibrium parameter concentration are derived in the proof.

The projection step can be read directly from any coupling \((X,Y)\) with laws \(\rho_k,\Pi_N\): \(\|p_\theta X-\theta_*\|_2\le\|X-Y\|_2+\|p_\theta Y-\theta_*\|_2\). The second term is controlled by concentration, and taking the infimum of the first gives transport. The shared Gaussian theorem bounds that transport. Consequently the three terms are added after all laws and moments have been identified, rather than assuming a separate parameter convergence estimate.

steps.title: Include every zero-dimensional case in the public theorem
steps.body:
The public theorem splits on whether the state coordinate index type is nonempty. In the nonempty case, instantiate the preceding theorem directly, retaining arbitrary independent \(d_\theta,d_x\). If the index type is empty, its parameter part forces \(d_\theta=0\); since \(N>0\), a positive \(d_x\) would supply a latent coordinate, so \(d_x=0\) as well. Normalize the Gibbs target by the same strong-convexity theorem and apply the singleton-state bound, where every error, transport distance and dimension term vanishes. This completes the displayed estimate in all dimensions. Existence and uniqueness of a permissible \(\theta_*\) are established separately by existsUnique_marginalMaximizer, so the maximizer binder does not demand an unproved existence assumption.

Formal correspondence: theorem1 : Strongly convex IPLA for independent, arbitrary parameter and latent dimensions. All stationary-reference and concentration inputs are derived. The zero-dimensional cases are included without extra assumptions.

The full-state index is empty precisely when both dimensions vanish, provided \(N>0\). If parameter dimension is positive there is a parameter coordinate; if latent dimension is positive there is a coordinate in any one of the nonempty particle blocks. Thus every remaining case belongs to the nonempty-state analytic theorem. The singleton case has zero parameter error and zero transport, giving exactly the same public formula without an implicit dimension restriction.

IPLA/LSI/Scaling.lean.title: Exact entropy scaling with an explicit lifted LSI constant
IPLA/LSI/Scaling.lean.summary:
Relative entropy is measured first on the full enlarged state. Dividing it by particle count produces a separate intensive quantity. The calculations below track both quantities, including their initial terms and forcing constants, under the physical-time substitution. The actual enlarged-target logarithmic Sobolev constant is retained throughout rather than inferred from an unrelated one-pair target.

Keep the LSI constant \(\beta\) of the actual lifted target explicit. Substitute \(h=\gamma/N\), \(\ell=NL\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\) into the shared ULA entropy argument. The regime \(\beta=N\alpha\) is an additional lifted-target assumption, with its own scalar specializations.

steps.title: Translate the numerical step and compatibility conditions
steps.body:
For \(N>0\), \(L>0\), factor the denominator and cancel positive \(N\) to get

\[\frac\gamma N\le\frac\beta{4(NL)^2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma\le\frac\beta{4NL^2}.\]

If \(\beta=N\alpha\), multiplication by positive \(N\) gives \(N\alpha\le NL\Longleftrightarrow\alpha\le L\), and cancellation gives \(N\alpha/(4NL^2)=\alpha/(4L^2)\). The forward compatibility lemma simply uses the equivalence. These are exact ordered-field identities; they do not derive an LSI for the lifted model from any pair-model LSI.

The general lifted theorem uses \(h=\gamma/N\), score constant \(L_N=NL\), dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and an LSI constant \(\beta\) for the actual lifted Gibbs target. Thus \(h\le\beta/(4L_N^2)\) becomes \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\). Only after additionally assuming \(\beta=N\alpha\) can the step restriction simplify to \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Positive \(N\) justifies these cancellations; no product tensorization is used, since the pair potentials share a parameter.

Formal correspondence: lifted_lsi_step_iff : The ULA restriction for the lifted step is exactly this IPLA restriction. linear_lsi_compatibility_iff : The scaled compatibility condition is equivalent to the base comparison. linear_lsi_step_iff : When the actual lifted LSI constant is N * alpha , the IPLA step restriction has no remaining particle-number factor.

The smoothness constant is squared in the entropy step restriction, so lifting introduces \(N^2\) in its denominator. The Euler step contributes one compensating factor \(1/N\); the physical restriction consequently retains one factor \(N\). If the target's LSI constant also grows as \(N\), that last factor cancels. These are numerical equivalences under positive denominators and should be separated from proving any functional inequality.

steps.title: Rewrite the contraction exponent
steps.body:
Associativity of real multiplication and division gives \(-\beta(\gamma/N)k=-\beta\gamma k/N\), so the corresponding exponentials agree. When \(\beta=N\alpha\) and \(N>0\), cancellation yields

\[e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}=e^{-\alpha\gamma k},\qquad e^{-(N\alpha)(\gamma/N)k}=e^{-\alpha\gamma k}.\]

The second version composes the first two identities. The rate becomes independent of \(N\) only under this explicitly supplied linear scaling of the actual lifted LSI constant.

Formal correspondence: lifted_entropy_rate_eq : The general decay rate retains the actual lifted LSI constant. linear_entropy_rate_eq : The rewritten general rate simplifies under the additional linear LSI scaling assumption. linear_ula_entropy_rate_eq : The same simplification directly from the ULA step notation.

At one iteration, the damping exponent is \(\beta h\). After \(k\) iterations it is \(\beta hk\), corresponding to the elapsed lifted time. Physical time is \(k\gamma\), so the effective entropy decay per physical unit is \(\beta/N\). Only a supplied lower bound of order \(N\) for the enlarged-target LSI constant makes this rate uniform in particle count.

steps.title: Rewrite full and normalized entropy biases
steps.body:
The shared ULA bias is \(8hD\ell^2/\beta\). Substitute the lifted values and cancel one particle factor:

\[\frac{8(\gamma/N)D(NL)^2}{\beta}=\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta},\qquad \frac1N\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}=\frac{8\gamma DL^2}{\beta}.\]

The dimension identity \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) follows by distributing division over the sum. If \(\beta=N\alpha\), the normalized bias becomes

\[\frac{8\gamma DL^2}{N\alpha}=\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The formal algebra handles \(\alpha=0\) separately because real division is total; applications use \(\alpha>0\). For any bound \(H\le qH_0+8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\), divide by positive \(N\), distribute, and use the second identity to obtain the normalized entropy bound.

The full-state bias is \(8hDL_N^2/\beta=8\gamma NDL^2/\beta\); dividing entropy by \(N\) removes exactly one particle factor. Under \(\beta=N\alpha\), its intensive form becomes \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). The initial entropy is divided by \(N\) at the same time. The one-step forcing is different: \(6h^2DL_N^2=6\gamma^2DL^2\), so its normalized form is \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). Keeping these full and intensive quantities separate avoids losing a factor of \(N\).

Formal correspondence: lifted_entropy_bias_eq : The unnormalized entropy bias after substituting the lifted step and smoothness. The dimension D is kept as a scalar parameter. normalized_entropy_bias_eq : Dividing the entropy by the particle number cancels one bias factor. normalized_dimension_eq : The intensive dimension appearing in normalized entropy. linear_normalized_entropy_bias_eq : The normalized bias under an LSI constant N * alpha for the actual lift. normalize_entropy_bound : A general entropy bound can be divided by the positive particle number, with its initial contribution and bias both normalized exactly.

Normalization divides every term by the same positive \(N\). In particular it does not change the exponential factor and cannot leave the full initial entropy unchanged. The bias also contains \(D\), which itself grows with particle count. Rewriting \(D/N\) reveals the intensive dimension and permits a meaningful comparison of bounds at different particle counts under the additional linear-LSI assumption.

steps.title: Rewrite the one-step forcing and normalized recurrence
steps.body:
The squared step cancels both particle factors in the squared smoothness:

\[6(\gamma/N)^2D(NL)^2=6\gamma^2DL^2.\]

Dividing by \(N\) and substituting the intensive dimension gives \(6\gamma^2DL^2/N=6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). Thus any supplied lifted recurrence normalizes to

\[\frac{H_{k+1}}N\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}\frac{H_k}N+\frac{6\gamma^2DL^2}{N}.\]

This scalar helper explicitly assumes its recurrence. Its proof divides by positive \(N\), rewrites the exponential argument, and applies the forcing identity. Under \(\beta=N\alpha\), the rate and intensive-dimension identities give the specialized recurrence with rate \(e^{-\alpha\gamma}\) and forcing \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). The analytic theorem derives the recurrence separately from interpolation data.

Formal correspondence: lifted_entropy_forcing_eq : The unnormalized one-step forcing loses both particle factors from the squared step. normalized_entropy_forcing_eq : The normalized one-step forcing has the intensive dimension. normalize_lifted_entropy_recurrence : Normalizing the lifted one-step recurrence. Its analytic recurrence is an explicit premise; this theorem performs only scalar scaling. linear_normalized_entropy_recurrence : The normalized recurrence under the additional linear lifted-LSI scale.

The forcing belongs to a one-step recurrence and is quadratic in the step. The long-time floor is larger by the geometric denominator \(1-e^{-\beta h}\), of order \(\beta h\). This explains why the final bias is first order in the physical step even though the one-step error is second order. Scalar normalization preserves the recurrence; the analytic interpolation argument is what supplies it for actual laws.

IPLA/LSI/Theorem.lean.title: Conditional entropy convergence for the actual Gaussian particle laws
IPLA/LSI/Theorem.lean.summary:
For the conditional entropy route, the actual Euler interpolation is assumed to have the density, weak-equation, differentiability and integrability properties needed for entropy calculus. These explicit analytic assumptions connect density calculations with the actual Gaussian algorithm laws. The proof derives finite entropy, the one-step recurrence and its geometric summation from those properties and the enlarged-target LSI.

Let \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and \(\Pi_N\propto e^{-V_N}\). Assume differentiability and \(L\)-Lipschitz joint gradient, an LSI of constant \(\beta>0\) for this actual target, \(\beta\le NL\), and \(0<\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\). Take an initial probability law \(\mu_0\). The endpoint also assumes RegularInterpolationData for \((V_N,\beta,\gamma/N,NL,\mu_0)\). These density, weak-equation, energy and moment obligations remain conditional; they have not been constructed from LSI and smoothness alone.

steps.title: The canonical particle laws are the actual Gaussian algorithm laws
steps.body:
Define \(\rho_k=\mu_0K_{\gamma/N}^{\,k}\); at \(k=0\) this is \(\mu_0\) by the iterate definition. The lifted gradient is \(NL\)-Lipschitz, so the measurable Gaussian transition preserves probability, and induction through the shared ULA law theorem proves \(\rho_k\) is a probability for every \(k\). If \(\mu_0\) is the initial law of the explicit independent-Gaussian IPLA recursion, laws_eq_ulaLawStep identifies it with this same iterate. Thus the entropy result concerns the actual algorithm rather than a substituted reference process.

Formal correspondence: particleLaws : The canonical Markov laws of IPLA, using its proved lifted-ULA transition. particleLaws_isProbability : The actual lifted IPLA transition preserves probability mass. particleLaws_eq_laws : These Markov laws agree with the existing noise-driven Gaussian IPLA realization, including its scalar coordinate laws and independence.

The Gaussian transition is a measurable image of the product of the current law and one independent standard vector. Its total mass is therefore one. Applying it repeatedly defines genuine probability laws without any stationarity assumption. Independence of the supplied innovation path identifies these same laws with the explicit particle recursion, so the entropy estimate concerns its current distribution at each finite iteration.

steps.title: Density regularity proves finite actual KL before real conversion
steps.body:
The LSI assumption includes that \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure. The interpolation data give positive relative densities \(r_k(t)\) with \(r_k(t)\Pi_N\) equal to the actual frozen-drift interpolation law, together with local entropy regularity and spatial smoothness. The shared finiteness theorem applies with \(h=\gamma/N\ge0\) and proves

\[\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N)<\infty\quad\text{for every }k.\]

The time-zero interpolation identity transfers this density-level KL finiteness to the actual iterate. In the probability-law application, the integrable entropy density also equals that actual finite KL. This guard precedes every use of toReal; infinite divergence is never turned into an artificial zero. The proof requires the supplied regularity, not a strong-convexity premise.

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_finite : The identified regular interpolation gives finite actual IPLA relative entropy. Target normalization follows from the lifted LSI assumption.

For a relative density \(r\), entropy is \(\int r\log r\,d\Pi_N\) when this quantity is integrable. The assumptions ensure that the interpolation density represents the Euler law at the relevant interval endpoint and that its entropy is finite. Equality of endpoint measures then transfers this finiteness to \(\rho_k\). This step is logically prior to treating the divergence as an ordinary real number in a differential or scalar recurrence.

steps.title: Derive entropy production and the one-step inequality
steps.body:
Put \(h=\gamma/N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N)\). The data provide the weak interpolation equation, differentiation and integration regularity, an error field \(e_k(t)\), and the bounds

\[\int r_k(t)\|e_k(t)\|^2d\Pi_N\le t^2\ell^2G_k+2tD\ell^2,\qquad G_k\le\frac{4\ell^2}{\beta}H_k+2D\ell.\]

The shared calculus tests the weak equation against the logarithmic density and uses Young's inequality to derive \(H'(t)\le-3J(t)/4+\int r\|e\|^2d\Pi_N\). LSI gives \(J(t)\ge2\beta H(t)\). Since \(h\le\beta/(4\ell^2)\) and \(\beta\le\ell\), one has \(h\ell\le1/4\) and \(\beta h\le1/4\). The error bounds then imply

\[H'(t)\le-\frac32\beta H(t)+\frac\beta4H_k+\frac52hD\ell^2.\]

The shared affine differential comparison and \(e^{-3x/2}+x/4\le e^{-x}\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\) give \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta h}H_k+6h^2D\ell^2\). The IPLA proof checks positivity of \(L\) from \(0<\beta\le NL\), translates the step restriction, and substitutes the exact lifted dimension and forcing. Therefore

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}H_k+6\gamma^2DL^2.\]

Dividing by positive \(N\) gives the normalized recurrence with forcing \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). Neither recurrence is a field of the interpolation structure.

Let \(H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N)\). The canonical laws are those of the actual lifted Gaussian Euler kernel, and the law identity relates them to the supplied realization. The regular interpolation data connect the density at both endpoints of every Euler interval to these same laws, and supply the analytic weak-equation and moment regularity used by the shared entropy theorem. Finite KL is proved before toReal is used.

Apply that theorem with \(h=\gamma/N\), \(L_N=NL\), dimension \(D\), and actual lifted LSI constant \(\beta\). The compatibility and positive-step facts are established by hL, hLs, hβLs and hscaled. The result is \[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}H_k+6\gamma^2DL^2.\] The normalized declaration divides this proved inequality by positive \(N\) and substitutes \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\).

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_one_step : The one-step entropy recurrence is derived from the regular weak interpolation equation. The forcing is 6 * gamma² * D * L² in the full state. particle_kl_one_step_normalized : The actual one-step recurrence per particle has the intensive dimension dx + dtheta / N .

The error field measures the difference between the true Langevin drift and the frozen Euler drift over one interval. Young's inequality absorbs part of its pairing with the density score into Fisher information. The LSI converts the remaining Fisher-information dissipation into entropy decay. The step restriction ensures the drift-error contribution proportional to the old entropy is small enough to preserve a strict contraction, leaving the explicit dimension-dependent forcing.

steps.title: Iterate and simplify the finite-entropy bound
steps.body:
Let \(q=e^{-\beta h}\). Repeated substitution in the one-step estimate gives

\[H_k\le q^kH_0+6h^2D\ell^2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j.\]

Because \(0<\beta h\le1/4\), the elementary bound \(1-e^{-\beta h}\ge3\beta h/4\) bounds the geometric sum by \(4/(3\beta h)\). Thus the shared theorem proves \(H_k\le e^{-\beta hk}H_0+8hD\ell^2/\beta\). Substitute \(h=\gamma/N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\) to obtain

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The proof invokes the shared bound after deriving every lifted numerical and regularity input, then uses the exact scaling identities. Dividing the entire inequality by positive \(N\) yields

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma DL^2}{\beta}.\]

Iterating the finite-entropy inequality uses the shared ULA entropy bound, whose geometric sum is controlled with the positive exponent \(\beta h\). After the exact lifted substitutions it yields \[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma NDL^2}{\beta}.\] The normalized result divides both the initial term and bias by \(N\). The linear-LSI specialization then substitutes the additional lifted hypothesis \(\operatorname{LSI}(\Pi_N,N\alpha)\), producing rate \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\) and intensive dimension \(d_x+d_\theta/N\). The Gaussian realization corollaries use equality of laws; they introduce no new entropy inequality.

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_bound : The shared ULA entropy argument in IPLA coordinates. The LSI constant beta belongs to the full lifted target; in particular it is not assumed to equal N times a pair-target constant. particle_kl_bound_normalized : Dividing the full-state relative entropy by the particle number gives its natural per-particle normalization.

Repeated substitution gives a finite geometric series with a nonnegative ratio strictly smaller than one. Its denominator is positive because \(\beta,h>0\). The elementary lower bound on \(1-e^{-\beta h}\) converts the quadratic forcing to the displayed linear-step floor. No passage to an infinite-time limit is needed: the same floor bounds the finite sum for every finite \(k\), while the initial contribution retains its exact exponential factor.

steps.title: Specialize only when the lifted target supplies β = Nα
steps.body:
Assume the actual lifted target has the supplied LSI constant \(N\alpha\), with \(0<\alpha\le L\), and \(0<\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Then \(N\alpha>0\), compatibility \(N\alpha\le NL\) holds, and the step equivalence supplies the general theorem's restriction. Its rate cancels to \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\); the normalized bias uses \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\). Consequently

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

This is a specialization of a lifted-target LSI already given in the hypotheses. The shared parameter makes the lifted model nonproduct, so no pair-target LSI tensorization is inferred.

Formal correspondence: particle_kl_bound_of_linear_lsi : If the lifted target actually has LSI constant N * alpha , the rate is independent of N and the normalized dimension is dx + dtheta / N . This is a specialization of a supplied lifted-target LSI, rather than a tensorization assertion about the original pair model.

Setting \(\beta=N\alpha\) in the general theorem changes both the admissible physical step and the decay rate. Dividing by \(N\) then expresses the floor using \(d_x+d_\theta/N\). The shared parameter prevents treating the enlarged Gibbs distribution as independent pair targets, so linear growth of its LSI strength remains a stated premise. The resulting specialization is valid whenever that premise is actually available.

steps.title: Transfer the canonical bounds to the supplied Gaussian realization
steps.body:
For a square-integrable initialization on \(P\) and noises satisfying all scalar Gaussian and independence fields, the law identity gives \(\rho_k=\operatorname{laws}(P,U,\gamma,k)\). Rewriting the normalized general bound by this equality proves the first Gaussian realization corollary. Rewriting the specialized \(N\alpha\)-LSI bound proves the second one, with all algorithm and interpolation assumptions retained. The entropy on the right is the full initial joint divergence relative to \(\Pi_N\); normalization divides both it and the subsequent joint divergence by \(N\). These conclusions by themselves do not assert parameter concentration about a mode.

Formal correspondence: gaussian_ipla_kl_bound_normalized : The normalized bound for the original independent-Gaussian IPLA realization. It is obtained by identifying its laws with particleLaws . gaussian_ipla_kl_bound_of_linear_lsi : The N * alpha lifted-LSI specialization for the actual Gaussian IPLA realization, with every algorithm-law assumption retained.

Relative entropy depends only on two measures, so equality of output laws is sufficient to transfer every conclusion. The initial joint law is also the same under this identification. Thus neither its entropy nor its normalization changes when replacing the canonical product realization by a supplied Gaussian realization. The interpolation assumptions remain attached to the same Euler laws, and no extra entropy inequality is introduced by this transfer.

IPLA/LSI/Marginal.lean.title: Parameter KL by data processing and guarded real conversion
IPLA/LSI/Marginal.lean.summary:
For entropy, projecting onto the parameter block requires only measurable data processing. No explicit formula for the parameter density is needed. This route therefore applies under the enlarged-target LSI assumptions even when no strong-convexity argument or concentration about a likelihood maximizer is available.

The parameter reference law is exactly the projection of the actual lifted Gibbs target. Measurable projection decreases extended KL, and finite joint KL makes the real bound transfer valid. This measure-theoretic argument needs no marginal-density or strong-convexity formula.

steps.title: Define the projected target and prove its probability property
steps.body:
With \(p=p_\theta\), define \(\Pi_N^\theta=p_\#\Pi_N\). The projection is a continuous linear map, hence measurable. For any probability measure \(\mu\), \((p_\#\mu)(\mathbb R^{d_\theta})=\mu(p^{-1}(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}))=\mu(\mathbb R^D)=1\). This proves probability preservation for any state law and then for the named target whenever \(\Pi_N\) is a probability. In the conditional LSI application that normalization comes from the LSI assumption itself.

Formal correspondence: parameterTarget : The parameter target is the actual lifted Gibbs law projected to its parameter coordinates. Probability normalization remains an explicit premise. parameterLaw_isProbability : Projecting a probability-valued state law preserves probability mass. parameterTarget_isProbability : The Gibbs parameter target is normalized whenever the actual joint target is normalized. No concentration or convexity hypothesis is introduced.

Pushforward preserves probability because the inverse image of the whole target space is the whole source space. The definition \(\Pi_N^\theta=(p_\theta)_\#\Pi_N\) therefore fixes a genuine parameter reference law whenever the joint target is normalized. It need not be described by a marginal potential for the entropy argument. The same observation applies to the current particle-state law and its parameter projection.

steps.title: Extended KL decreases under the parameter projection
steps.body:
The shared data-processing theorem for a measurable map yields

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert p_\# u)\le\operatorname{KL}(\mu\Vert u).\]

At the density level this is convexity of \(u\log u\) under averaging over forgotten coordinates; the measure theorem does not require a constructed conditional density. If the right-hand divergence is finite, the inequality immediately excludes infinity on the left. Since both extended quantities are finite, order is preserved when taking their real values. This proves the real data-processing inequality with its necessary finiteness guard.

The parameter projection is a continuous linear map and hence measurable. Data processing gives the extended inequality \(\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert p_\# u)\le\operatorname{KL}(\mu\Vert u)\) before any real conversion. A finite joint KL therefore proves finite marginal KL, and only then can ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal transfer the order. This is a divergence statement about the actual pushed-forward target, with no density formula or optimizer concentration assumed.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_le_joint : Extended-valued data processing for the common parameter projection. parameter_kl_ne_top_of_joint : Finite joint KL implies finite parameter KL. parameter_klReal_le_joint : The real data-processing inequality, with finiteness of both divergences established before taking their toReal values.

Data processing averages out information in the discarded particle coordinates. Convexity of the entropy integrand makes this averaging nonincreasing for divergence. The resulting extended inequality remains meaningful if the joint divergence is infinite. For a finite numerical estimate, the joint entropy theorem first excludes that case; the projected divergence is then finite as well and both sides can be read as real numbers.

steps.title: Transfer a full-joint or per-particle bound with the correct factor
steps.body:
If finite full joint KL has real bound \(H\le B\), transitivity with real data processing gives parameter KL at most \(B\). If instead \(H/N\le B\) and \(N>0\), multiplication by the positive count yields \(H\le NB\), hence

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert p_\#\nu)\le NB.\]

The proof uses the positive-denominator order equivalence before applying the full-joint transfer lemma. This factor is necessary because normalized joint entropy is not the same quantity as parameter-marginal entropy.

If the available estimate is intensive, \(H/N\le B\), positive \(N\) gives the full joint bound \(H\le NB\), and data processing then gives marginal KL at most \(NB\). It does not give marginal KL at most \(B\). The initial entropy in the final bound is still full joint entropy: projection decreases initial entropy, so replacing that term by initial parameter entropy would make the right-hand side smaller without a supporting argument.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_bound_of_joint_bound : Any finite real bound on full joint KL is also a parameter-marginal bound. parameter_kl_bound_of_per_particle_bound : A per-particle joint entropy bound controls unscaled parameter KL after multiplication by the particle count.

If the available bound is \(H_k/N\le B_k\), multiplication gives \(H_k\le NB_k\). Combining it with parameter data processing yields \(H_k^\theta\le NB_k\), not \(B_k\). The same reasoning explains why the full initial entropy persists in the parameter theorem: the joint evolution was controlled using that initial quantity, and the projection inequality alone gives no replacement of it by a smaller projected initial value.

steps.title: Specialize all transfers to the actual Gibbs parameter target
steps.body:
Set \(\nu=\Pi_N\) in the three generic statements. By the definition of \(\Pi_N^\theta\), this yields extended data processing \(\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\mu\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le\operatorname{KL}(\mu\Vert\Pi_N)\), finiteness of parameter KL whenever joint KL is finite, and any real upper-bound transfer. The proofs are direct specializations and retain normalization of both laws and the finite-joint guard. No additional concentration or optimizer estimate appears in this measure projection step.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_le_gibbs_joint : Extended KL data processing with the actual Gibbs parameter target. parameter_kl_ne_top_of_gibbs_joint : Finite actual Gibbs-relative joint KL gives finite parameter KL. parameter_kl_bound_of_gibbs_joint_bound : A joint KL estimate transfers to the actual Gibbs parameter marginal, without constructing a formula for its marginal density.

Both measures in data processing must be projected by the same map. Using the actual Gibbs projection ensures that the reference in the parameter conclusion corresponds exactly to the reference in the joint theorem. The probability and finiteness hypotheses are inherited from that theorem. Consequently the specialization adds no density regularity, independence or optimizer assumption beyond those already used to control the joint law.

IPLA/LSI/Corollaries.lean.title: Conditional entropy bounds for the actual parameter marginal
IPLA/LSI/Corollaries.lean.summary:
The parameter conclusions combine two previously established facts: finite entropy and a quantitative bound for the joint Euler law, and monotonicity of divergence under the parameter projection. The complete initial joint entropy and any factor arising from per-particle normalization are retained in every resulting inequality.

Combine the finite joint entropy result with measurable parameter projection. Every conclusion retains the lifted-target LSI and the explicit regular interpolation data. The initialization term remains the full joint initial divergence.

steps.title: The actual parameter divergence is finite
steps.body:
The particle-law probability theorem proves \(\rho_k\) is a probability, and the LSI hypothesis proves \(\Pi_N\) is a probability. The supplied interpolation data prove finite actual joint KL for \(\gamma\ge0\). Apply the Gibbs-specific finiteness transfer to obtain \(\operatorname{KL}(p_{\theta\#}\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)<\infty\). This is an extended-valued assertion, proved before any real-valued inequality.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_finite : Finite actual joint IPLA KL supplies finite actual parameter KL.

The finite joint entropy inequality already places the current law in the finite-divergence domain relative to the target. Data processing maps this domain into the corresponding parameter finite-divergence domain. This proves the existence of a finite parameter entropy before assigning a numerical upper bound to it. Probability normalization of both laws is inherited from the actual Markov transition and the stated target LSI.

steps.title: Transfer the full general joint bound
steps.body:
Under \(N>0\), \(\beta>0\), \(\beta\le NL\), and \(0<\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\), the joint theorem gives \(H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\). The finite joint guard and the Gibbs projection bound yield

\[\operatorname{KL}(p_{\theta\#}\rho_k\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

Both probability properties are established within the proof. Here \(H_0=\operatorname{KL}(\mu_0\Vert\Pi_N)\), rather than the smaller projected initial divergence; data processing does not permit replacing the initial term in this argument.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_bound : The actual parameter marginal inherits the full joint KL bound for any supplied lifted LSI constant beta . The initial entropy is the full joint entropy.

Apply data processing at the same iteration \(k\), then substitute the full joint bound. Its initial term measures information in both the parameter and particles. The exponential and bias are unchanged because projection only decreases the left side. This argument controls divergence between parameter probability laws; it does not convert that divergence into distance from a deterministic maximizing parameter.

steps.title: Retain N when using the normalized linear-LSI bound
steps.body:
If the actual lifted LSI constant is \(N\alpha\), the normalized joint theorem gives

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The per-particle transfer lemma multiplies this complete upper bound by positive \(N\), so the unscaled parameter divergence is at most

\[N\left[e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right)\right].\]

The proof obtains finite joint KL separately and then applies this guarded transfer. This entropy estimate compares two parameter probability laws; no concentration at a marginal-likelihood maximizer is asserted.

The proof first installs probability instances for the actual particle law and Gibbs target, using kernel mass preservation and the LSI hypothesis's normalization field. It next supplies the proved finite joint KL to the real data-processing theorem. In the general case it transfers the full joint bound directly. In the \(N\alpha\) case it transfers the normalized bound by multiplying its entire right side by \(N\): \[\operatorname{KL}(p_\#\rho_k\Vert p_\#\Pi_N)\le N\left[e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}(d_x+d_\theta/N)\right].\] The lifted LSI and regular interpolation hypotheses remain exactly those of the joint theorem.

Formal correspondence: parameter_kl_bound_of_linear_lsi : Under the supplied lifted LSI constant N * alpha , the normalized joint entropy estimate bounds unscaled parameter KL only after multiplication by N . This does not replace the initial joint entropy with initial parameter entropy.

Under the linear-LSI specialization, start from the intensive estimate and undo its normalization before projecting. Multiplying the complete right side by \(N\) restores the initial entropy \(H_0\) and produces bias \(8\gamma L^2D/\alpha\). This is consistent with substituting \(\beta=N\alpha\) directly into the full theorem. Agreement of the two routes checks the particle factors in the corollary.

IPLA/ReferenceFamily.lean.summary:
Transport distance is an infimum of coupling costs. To obtain an initial Wasserstein term from a synchronous process estimate, one must construct the reference for arbitrary finite-cost initial couplings and show that its algorithm marginal is independent of the chosen coupling. These are the two substantive requirements of the initial-coupling argument.

steps.title: Take the infimum without assuming an optimal coupling
steps.body:

Its fields require that the initial \(L^2\) difference be at most \(\operatorname{cost}(c)\), and that every realization produce the same output law \(\mu_k\). The shared coupling theorem gives \(W_2(\mu_k,\pi)\le q^k\operatorname{cost}(c)+b\) for each such \(c\). Taking the cost infimum yields \(q^kW_2(\mu_0,\pi)+b\). A finite-cost coupling also proves output finiteness before real conversion. steps.title: Minkowski on each coupling gives the projected RMS estimate
steps.body:
For a linear contraction \(T\), any center \(b\), and a coupling \(c\) of \(\mu,\pi\), write \(Tx-b=T(x-y)+(Ty-b)\). Minkowski and \(\|T(x-y)\|\le\|x-y\|\) imply

\[\|Tx-b\|_{L^2(\mu)}\le\operatorname{cost}(c)+\|Ty-b\|_{L^2(\pi)}.\]

Taking the infimum over couplings proves the same inequality with \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\). Finite transport plus a finite equilibrium radius proves finiteness of the projected moment. Only then does the shared real conversion identify its value with \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu}\). A second-moment bound at equilibrium supplies the concentration radius. No optimal coupling or separate Wasserstein triangle inequality is needed.

steps.title: Join integral solutions and identify their Euler noises
steps.body:
For each interval \([kh,(k+1)h]\), solve the Lipschitz-drift integral equation in \(L^2\), starting from the preceding endpoint:

\[Y_{k,t}-Y_{k,0}=-\int_0^t\nabla V(Y_{k,s})ds+\sqrt2\bigl(B_{kh+t}-B_{kh}\bigr).\]

The construction proves continuity, the initial value and interval joining. Normalize each Brownian endpoint by \(\sqrt{2h}\) to obtain the same Euler noise vector, and use Gaussian second moments to get the noise norm \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). Given the explicit all-time Gibbs-law premise, the Gibbs score bound yields \(\|\nabla V(Y_{k,t})\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld}\), assembling the shared integral-reference structure. This layer keeps stationarity visible as a premise, rather than claiming the construction alone proves it.

steps.title: Separate initialization from the noise source
steps.body:
On \((H\times H)\times S\) with law \(c\otimes Q\), let the two initial variables be the first and second coordinates of \(c\), and let every innovation depend only on \(S\). Product independence makes both initial variables independent of the noise source. The first chain evolves by \(x\mapsto x-h\nabla V(x)+\sqrt{2h}\xi_k\), and its output law is the pushforward of \(\mu_0\otimes Q\) by the measurable recursion; hence it depends only on \(\mu_0\), not on the chosen coupling \(c\). This verifies the common-output obligation needed to take the coupling infimum. Finite coupling cost and Gibbs moments supply the \(L^2\) initial realization; the proved output finiteness justifies the subsequent real-valued transport bounds.

steps.title: Brownian source, product pullback and Gaussian innovations

Pulling a Brownian coordinate through the measure-preserving source projection preserves its Brownian law. Define the source Euler coordinates by

\[\xi_{k,a}=\frac{B_a((k+1)h)-B_a(kh)}{\sqrt h},\qquad h>0.\]

Gaussian increment laws give unit variance, and coordinate independence plus independent disjoint increments give independence in both \(k\) and \(a\). steps.title: Finite joint entropy and the full IPLA bound
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\). Assume differentiable \(U\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, a genuine LSI with constant \(\beta>0\) for the actual lifted Gibbs target \(\Pi_N\), a positive step \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\), and finite initial joint entropy \(H_0\). Then every actual particle law has finite KL and

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The lifted potential is differentiable and has \(NL\)-Lipschitz gradient. The particle law is exactly its ULA law with step \(h=\gamma/N\). The step equivalence gives \(h\le\beta/(4(NL)^2)\), so the shared unconditional ULA theorem applies. Substituting \(h=\gamma/N\), dimension \(D\), and smoothness \(NL\) transforms its rate into \(e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\) and its bias into \(8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\). The proof derives positive \(L\) from the positive admissible step before dividing.

The shared theorem constructs all Gaussian interpolation and entropy calculus. Neither compatibility nor regular interpolation data is a premise here. Finiteness is retained as the first component of the conclusion, before real-valued KL is used.

The lifted substitution must be made in both occurrences of smoothness: \(\ell^2=N^2L^2\), while \(h=\gamma/N\). Thus the step restriction becomes \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) and the bias becomes \(8\gamma NDL^2/\beta\). Equality of the Gaussian Euler and particle laws transfers these conclusions to the algorithm. Finite entropy is kept alongside the estimate so every real divergence appearing in the formula is justified.

steps.title: Normalize the full joint entropy
steps.body:
Start with the finite full-state entropy theorem. Divide its real inequality by the positive number \(N\), preserving the inequality direction:

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma D L^2}{\beta}.\]

The helper normalize_entropy_bound divides both the initial contribution and the bias, canceling one particle factor in the latter. The same finite-KL witness is retained for the unnormalized divergence. This quantity is the entropy of the full state divided by particle number; parameter projection is handled separately.

Since \(N>0\), division preserves the order and gives the same exponential multiplying the intensive initial entropy. The full divergence remains a finite property of the original law; only its numerical normalization has changed. This per-particle quantity is useful for comparing enlarged systems of different size, but it is not itself the entropy of the parameter marginal.

steps.title: An actual lifted LSI of strength N alpha
steps.body:
Suppose the actual lifted target satisfies LSI with constant \(\beta=N\alpha\), where \(\alpha>0\). The positive particle count gives \(\beta>0\), and the step equivalence simplifies \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) to \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Apply the unconditional normalized theorem at this lifted constant.

The rate simplifies to \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\). Since \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\), its normalized bias becomes \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). Thus

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The LSI premise is for \(\Pi_N\) itself. The proof performs these exact substitutions and retains finite output KL; it does not infer the lifted LSI by tensorizing a parameter–latent pair model.

The additional LSI premise has to concern the actual coupled particle target. Its substitution cancels the particle factor in the exponential and combines the normalized dimension as \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\). Consequently the intensive floor has a finite latent-dimension term at fixed physical step. The argument performs these cancellations after invoking the constructed joint theorem and does not invoke pairwise product tensorization.

steps.title: Project the actual joint law to the parameter
steps.body:
Apply the parameter projection to the actual particle law and to the same lifted Gibbs target. KL data processing gives \(\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le H_k\). The unconditional joint theorem first supplies \(H_k<\infty\), which also proves finiteness of the projected KL before real conversion.

Transitivity with the full joint estimate yields
